newsitem.title: USA: U.S. fed cattle numbers seen above year ago.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fed cattle numbers seen above year ago.

text.p: The number of cattle in major U.S. feedlots is again projected to exceed last year's levels as moderate January placements compare with light placements last year, livestock analysts said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department is expected to confirm the expected rise in fed supplies on Friday in its monthly Cattle on Feed report, set for release at 1400 CST/2000 GMT.

Analysts project the data will show cattle on feed numbers for feedlots of 1,000 head or more capacity in the seven key states on February 1 at an average 103.9 percent of a year ago, in a range of 101.5 to 105.4.

January placement data will likely be the most important part of the report as analyst estimates ranged widely. Estimates averaged 107.5 percent of a year ago in a Reuter pre-report survey, ranging from 99.0 to 114.6 percent.

Don Close, senior livestock analyst for Pioneer Hi-Bred, estimated that placements would be up 10 percent from last year and said profitability was a big reason for feedlots to be aggressive in placing feeders onto feed during January.
"In January (feedlots) were still profitable -- you were still buying feeders that had attractive prospective break-evens," Close said.

Analysts pointed out that placements were light last year during January and this accounts for some of the high percentage estimates. However, the number going onto feedlots is still large for the time period.
"It's (placements) going to be a pretty big number, well over 100,000 above the five-year average," said Tom Tippens, CEO of Professional Cattle Consultants Inc.
Placements were heavier in the early part of January compared to later in the month. The trend for lighter placements then carried over into February, they said.
"We continued to rally feeder cattle prices and then we started to see, for the past four to six weeks, fed cattle prices decline" and this has cut placements, Close added.
Some analysts also thought that placements were not that heavy during January as many of the cattle that were moving around actually were going from one pasture area to another.
"I believe a lot of the cattle that moved were actually moving to go back out to grass," said Dale Benson, Vice President and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
Benson had the smallest estimate for January placements at 99 percent.
Analysts expect December marketing data to show fairly active feedlot sales as feedlots keep as current as possible. Marketing estimates averaged 101.3 percent, ranging from 99.0 to 104.0 percent.
"They are keeping the feedlots current," Benson said.

Analysts continued to estimate only the seven-state part of the report with feedlots over 1,000 head even though USDA began a 12-state report more than a year ago. More time was needed to compare historical data, they said.
